newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -- Disney sees 4-6 cruise ships on horizon.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- Disney sees 4-6 cruise ships on horizon.

text.p: The fledgling Disney Cruise Line, which began taking reservations on Monday, will be profitable by its second year and may eventually add ships off the U.S. West Coast and France, the head of the cruise unit said.

"There is absolutely no resistance in Disney to growing this business. There is no reason we couldn't have four to six ships in 10 years," Arthur Rodney, president of Disney Cruise Line, told Reuters in an interview.
"There's certainly a possibility we might some day have a ship on the U.S. West Coast, where Disney is building a new theme park, or in France near Euro Disney," he added.

Monday marked the first day that travel agents and consumers could book reservations for a Disney cruise. The company anticipates so much demand for its inaugural cruises in early 1998 that it plans to set up a lottery system to choose which paying customers get to board the ship.
Disney will launch its first ship, the Disney Magic, in April 1998 with three- and four-day cruises off the Florida coast.

The cruises are designed as an add-on package for families and couples at Walt Disney World near Orlando. But Rodney said he anticipated adding seven-day cruises during the first year of operations "because we have so much entertainment aboard these ships."
A second ship, the Disney Wonder, is due to be delivered at the end of 1998.
Cruise industry experts estimate that Disney spent more than $300 million to build each ship, plus at least $25 million to purchase and develop a private Bahamian island as a port of call.
"It's a sizable investment for the company," Rodney said, declining to give specific figures. "We're roughly equivalent to another theme park with these two ships and the island."

Rodney said the cruise line would be profitable in 1999, after its first full year of operations. "We expect to make a major contribution to this company, as well as to theme park stays, food and beverage sales and other revenue," he said.

Nearly half of the private island of 1,000 acres is being developed for vacationers to swim, fish, snorkel or sunbathe, Rodney said. "There's a possibility we might develop the remaining 600 acres. There are some thoughts of building a hotel there."

Analyst Jill Krutick of Smith Barney said the new cruise unit was part of a companywide strategy to develop attractions and resorts that keep families on its giant Walt Disney World property -- and spending money -- for their entire vacation.
"It will enhance the length of stay patterns," she said.
"It's another way of keeping people at Disney, just like another attraction at a park."

Disney Cruise Lines is charging premium prices for its packages, compared to the rest of the U.S. cruise industry which has struggled to fill the growing number of new ships being rolled out. A seven-day resort and cruise vacation begins at $1,229 per person for a cruise plus Disney's moderately priced hotels, and can range as high as $3,339 per person for a cruise and a stay at Disney's luxury hotels.
Disney being Disney, consumers can also expect to see the new cruise line burst onto the scene with joint marketing promotions with AT&T, McDonald's Corp and American Express.
"We don't have to do much in the way of brand recognition," Rodney said. "We'll have more entertainment on our ships than anyone else because we're an entertainment company."

The Disney ships will also differ from the rest of the industry by not having gambling casinos, and devoting nearly a full deck to childrens' activities. One area, the Oceaneer Club, is designed for kids aged three to eight and will offer character-themed games and a pirate ship. Another area, the Oceaneer Lab, is for nine to 12-year-olds with interactive media and high-tech games.

"Parents will be able to sign up their kids for activities from breakfast until 1 a.m. the next day if they wish," Rodney said. "Being Disney, we have to be better than everybody else with kids' entertainment."
